title: My condo is worth less than my loan. Sell at a loss or rent it out?
excerpt: An owner who moved to Singapore can't sell his Cyberjaya condo at the loan amount, and rent would cover only part of the instalment. Sean would take the loss and move on, if he can afford the gap.

question.asker: From Atwin, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Atwin bought a three-bedroom condo in Cyberjaya with no initial capital, to live in. The build quality turned out poor, and in 2021 he moved his family to Singapore. The SPA price was RM720,000 and the loan RM650,000, but the valuation is now about RM550,000. His instalment is about RM3,200 plus maintenance, while fully furnished units nearby rent for RM2,300 to RM2,500. Fixing it up to rent would cost RM20,000 to RM25,000.
question.text: If he mainly wants to sell, should he spend money to rent it out first, or just cut the price and sell?

answer.quote: We pay interest for things that are depreciating in value.
answer.summary: If he can afford the gap between the sale price and what he still owes, sell, accept the loss and put his credit and cash into a location with real demand. Only hold and furnish it to rent if he can't cover that gap, because there the rent will never exceed the instalment.

reasons.title: Judge it against the net price
reasons.body: With zero down payment and developer discounts, the real cost was the loan of about RM650,000, not the RM720,000 SPA price. Owners who compare a subsale price with the inflated SPA price think they have lost more than they have.

reasons.title: The buyer's bank lends on valuation
reasons.body: A buyer's loan is based on the valuation, so at RM550,000 anything above that must be paid in cash. Getting a valuation done sets a realistic price before you sell.

reasons.title: Work out the real gap first
reasons.body: After years of payments, mostly interest, the outstanding loan might be about RM600,000. Selling at RM550,000 would leave about RM50,000 to pay in cash, or as a personal loan, which many people end up taking.

reasons.title: Holding has a cost too
reasons.body: Renting at about RM2,500 still leaves him bleeding roughly RM1,000 a month on a unit Sean doesn't expect to appreciate. That money and borrowing power could go into areas with high search and transaction demand.

actions: Get a valuation and check your outstanding loan before setting a price.
If the shortfall is affordable, sell and reallocate your credit and cash to a stronger location.
If you can't cover the shortfall, furnish and rent the unit to cut the monthly loss while you wait.
Consider selling with a tenant in place, which widens the pool to investors, including younger buyers who can take a longer loan.
If managing the unit drains you, hand it to a property management company so tenants deal with them, not you.
caveat: Landed homes in Cyberjaya remain in demand; Sean's view is about high-rise units there. If you are moving to Singapore for good, also check how owning Malaysian property affects becoming a PR and buying an HDB flat.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #248. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in April 2024. The property management company Sean suggests is a sister company of the renovation business he works with.
